Wolman disease, also known as Wolman disease or Wolman's disease, is a rare genetic disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme lysosomal acid lipase (LAL). It is a form of lysosomal storage disease.

The exact prevalence of Wolman disease is not well-documented, but it is estimated to be extremely rare. According to the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the incidence of Wolman disease is about 1 in 500,000 to 1 in 1 million births.

There are only a few hundred reported cases of Wolman disease worldwide, and it is considered a very rare condition. The disease is usually diagnosed in infancy or early childhood, and it is often fatal within the first few years of life if left untreated.

It's worth noting that there are some variations of Wolman disease, including a milder form called cholesteryl ester storage disease (CESD), which may have a slightly higher prevalence. However, even in these cases, the disease is still considered rare.

The rarity of Wolman disease makes it challenging to determine the exact number of people affected, but it is generally agreed upon that it is a very rare condition.
